newsitem.title: USA: US industries would be harmed by carbon tax--study.
newsitem.headline: US industries would be harmed by carbon tax--study.

text.p: A draft of a study conducted by the U.S. Energy Department's Argonne National Laboratory said six major U.S. industries would be devastated if the United States boosted fuel prices as a way to combat global warming.

The study, made available by industry groups, also said imposing taxes on carbon content of fuel to reduce emissions of heat-trapping greenhouse gases would be "neither effective, nor cost-effective."

A spokesman for the White House Task Force on Climate Change said the administration was not considering a carbon tax, and said the Argonne study was not based on the administration's plan to encourage pollution reductions through a system of emission credit trading.

"The Argonne report is not something that is considered relevant to the analysis being done," the spokesman said, referring to the economic impact study the administration was preparing to support its climate change plan.
He said the Argonne study was started before the administration developed its emissions trading plan, which it has submitted in international talks on climate change.

Some industries that oppose the administration's call for binding commitments among industrialized countries to reduce heat-trapping pollution have said they feared the United States would turn to a carbon tax.

The Argonne study said a policy of higher fuel prices in the United States and other industrialized countries would result in major shifts of industries to developing countries that were not under contraints.

The study evaluated effects on chemicals, petroleum refining, paper and allied products, iron and steel, aluminum and cement -- industries it said would be most affected because they are large and highly energy-intensive.
The study was done by getting responses from industry experts, which were evaluated by working groups made up of industry, academic, government, labor and environmental representatives.

Each of the industy experts said higher fuel prices in the United States "would increase the cost of producing goods in these industries to a level above that of foreign non-participating competitors," the report said.
"As a result, imports from non-participating countries would increase and output and employment in domestic industries would be reduced," it said.
